turns.content: Hi, I'm working on an article about poverty and inequality in India and need some reliable data sources. Could you help me find clear statistics with proper citations that I can easily integrate into my report?
I encountered an error processing your request:
Could you please try again and provide the data sources along with API URLs and downloadable formats for easy integration?

I’m currently set up to work with a specific family of data tools (the “data360_*” World Bank tools) but they aren’t exposed in this environment, so I can’t directly click through and fetch indicator IDs or live API URLs for you. Instead, I’ll give you a practical, source-by-source guide with:

- Exact database/source names  
- Direct web links to browse/download data  
- API endpoints or patterns you can call programmatically  
- Notes on formats (CSV, Excel, JSON, etc.)  
- A few key India-relevant poverty/inequality indicators per source  

You can then plug these into your workflow or scripts.

---

## 1. World Bank – World Development Indicators (WDI)

**What it’s good for:** Long-run, internationally comparable series on poverty, inequality, growth, social indicators.

### Key India poverty/inequality indicators

- Poverty headcount ratio at $2.15 a day (2017 PPP) (% of population) – `SI.POV.DDAY`
- Poverty headcount ratio at $3.65 a day (2017 PPP) (% of population) – `SI.POV.LMIC`
- Poverty headcount ratio at $6.85 a day (2017 PPP) (% of population) – `SI.POV.UMIC`
- Gini index – `SI.POV.GINI`
- Income share held by lowest 10% – `SI.DST.10TH.10`
- Income share held by highest 10% – `SI.DST.10TH.10` (check metadata; there are several distribution indicators)
- Income share held by lowest 20% – `SI.DST.02ND.20`
- Income share held by highest 20% – `SI.DST.05TH.20`

Country code for India: `IND`.

### Web interface (downloadable files)

- Main portal:  
  https://databank.worldbank.org/source/world-development-indicators

From there you can:

- Select “India” as country
- Add the indicators above
- Download as:
  - CSV
  - Excel (XLSX)
  - XML

### API access

Base API docs:  
https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589-developer-information

**General pattern:**

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/{country_code}/indicator/{indicator}?format=json&per_page=2000
```

**Examples for India:**

- Gini index for India:

  ```text
  https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SI.POV.GINI?format=json&per_page=2000
  ```

- Poverty headcount at $2.15/day (2017 PPP):

  ```text
  https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SI.POV.DDAY?format=json&per_page=2000
  ```

You can change `format=` to:

- `json` – JSON (easy for scripts)
- `xml` – XML

**Quick Python example:**

```python
import requests

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SI.POV.DDAY"
params = {"format": "json", "per_page": 2000}
r = requests.get(url, params=params)
data = r.json()
```

**Citation format (example):**

> World Bank. World Development Indicators. “Poverty headcount ratio at $2.15 a day (2017 PPP) (% of population) [SI.POV.DDAY].” Accessed [date].  

---

## 2. World Bank – PovcalNet (Global Poverty Monitoring)

**What it’s good for:** Official World Bank global poverty estimates and micro-based distributions; more detailed than WDI for poverty.

### Web interface

- PovcalNet online tool:  
  https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/brief/povcalnet

It allows you to:

- Select India
- Choose poverty lines (e.g., $2.15, $3.65, $6.85)
- Get headcount ratios, gaps, mean income, etc.
- Download outputs as CSV or Excel.

### API access

API documentation:  
https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/brief/povcalnet-api

Typical API structure (GET):

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/povcalnet/povcalnet?country=IND&povertyline=2.15&year=all&format=json
```

Parameters:

- `country=IND`
- `povertyline=2.15` (or 3.65, 6.85, etc.)
- `year=all` or a specific year
- `format=json` or `csv`

**Example for all years, India, $2.15/day:**

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/povcalnet/povcalnet?country=IND&povertyline=2.15&year=all&format=csv
```

This returns a CSV you can download or feed directly into your workflow.

**Citation example:**

> World Bank. PovcalNet: the online tool for poverty measurement. India, poverty line $2.15 (2017 PPP). Accessed [date].  

---

## 3. World Bank – Global Database of Shared Prosperity (GDSP)

**What it’s good for:** Growth in incomes/consumption of the bottom 40% vs. average – a popular inequality/“shared prosperity” measure.

### Web / downloads

- Shared Prosperity portal:  
  https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/poverty/brief/shared-prosperity

The underlying data are often also exposed through WDI or downloadable spreadsheets linked from that page (typically Excel).

### API

Some shared prosperity indicators are available through the main World Bank API (as WDI or related indicators). Common codes include:

- Growth rate of household income or consumption per capita among the bottom 40% – often `SI.SPR.PCAP.ZG`
- Shared prosperity premium – `SI.SPR.PCAP.ZP` (naming can change; always verify in WDI)

Pattern:

```text
https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SI.SPR.PCAP.ZG?format=json&per_page=2000
```

---

## 4. World Inequality Database (WID)

**What it’s good for:** Top income shares, wealth inequality, long-run distributional series that often go beyond what WDI provides.

### Web interface

- WID main page:  
  https://wid.world
- Country page for India:  
  https://wid.world/country/india

You can interactively select:

- Pre-tax national income shares (top 1%, top 10%, bottom 50%)
- Wealth inequality
- Gini coefficients
- Time series

And download:

- CSV
- Excel
- Sometimes ready-made charts.

### API access

API documentation:  
https://wid.world/documentation/

Basic API endpoint pattern:

```text
https://wid.world/data/api/{indicator}/{area}/?downloadformat={format}
```

For India, the “area” code is usually `in` or `IND` depending on the series; WID’s documentation gives the exact codes. Example pattern:

```text
https://wid.world/data/api/shweal999i/in/?downloadformat=csv
```

Where:

- `shweal999i` – indicator code (e.g., share of wealth held by top 10%)
- `in` – India
- `downloadformat=csv` or `xlsx`

You’ll need to look up the exact indicator codes in their docs/interface for the specific series you need (top 1% income share, etc.).

**Citation example:**

> World Inequality Database (WID). “Distribution of national income and wealth – India.” Accessed [date].  

---

## 5. India – National Sample Survey / PLFS & Household Surveys (via MOSPI)

**What it’s good for:** Underlying microdata and official Indian statistics (consumption, employment, etc.). Great for original poverty/inequality analysis, but less plug-and-play than WDI.

### Main portals

- Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI):  
  https://www.mospi.gov.in
- National Sample Survey (NSS) / Household Consumption:  
  https://www.mospi.gov.in/national-sample-survey-office-nsso
- Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS):  
  https://www.mospi.gov.in/periodic-labour-force-survey-plfs

From these pages you can:

- Download published reports in PDF
- Often download data tables in Excel/CSV
- Apply for access to unit-level microdata (paid / restricted).

### API / machine-readable access

MOSPI has some open data via:

- Open Government Data (OGD) Platform India:  
  https://data.gov.in

Search for “poverty,” “consumption,” “NSS,” or “PLFS.” Many datasets are downloadable as:

- CSV
- JSON
- XML
- Excel

Each dataset page typically provides:

- Direct CSV download link
- JSON API endpoint (with query parameters for filters).

**Example of OGD API pattern:**

Each dataset has a resource ID; the API pattern is:

```text
https://api.data.gov.in/resource/{resource_id}?api-key={YOUR_API_KEY}&format=json&limit=1000
```

You’ll need to register for a (free) API key on data.gov.in.

**Citation example:**

> Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI). “Household Consumer Expenditure Survey, NSS [round/year].” Government of India. Accessed [date].  

---

## 6. India – NITI Aayog / SDG India Index & Poverty Dashboards

**What it’s good for:** State-level inequality and poverty-related indicators; SDG tracking (e.g., SDG 1 – No Poverty, SDG 10 – Reduced Inequalities).

### Web portals

- NITI Aayog data and SDG dashboard:  
  https://www.niti.gov.in  
  https://sdgindiaindex.niti.gov.in (URL sometimes changes; if broken, follow links from main site)

Data are typically downloadable as:

- Excel (XLSX)
- PDF (reports)
- Sometimes CSV.

### API / machine-readable

NITI Aayog does not have a universal public API like World Bank, but some SDG dashboards are hosted on platforms that expose JSON behind the scenes. For robust, citable data, it’s safer to:

- Use the official Excel/CSV downloads.
- Or, if you must scrape JSON, document that it is from the SDG dashboard and include the URL and access date.

**Citation example:**

> NITI Aayog. “SDG India Index – No Poverty (SDG 1) and Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10) indicators, India and States/UTs.” Government of India. Accessed [date].  

---

## 7. UNDP – Human Development Reports (HDR) & Inequality-Adjusted HDI

**What it’s good for:** High-level inequality measures (e.g., inequality-adjusted HDI, income inequality, multidimensional poverty index – MPI).

### Web interface and downloads

- Human Development Data Center:  
  https://hdr.undp.org/data-center

You can:

- Filter by country (India)
- Download datasets as:
  - CSV
  - Excel
  - Stata files in some cases

Key indicators:

- Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
- Headcount ratio (population in multidimensional poverty)
- Intensity of deprivation
- Inequality in income, education, life expectancy

### API

UNDP’s HDR data are primarily offered as bulk downloadable files rather than a stable public API. For programmatic integration, you typically:

- Download the global CSV/Excel
- Filter for India in your own code.

**Citation example:**

> United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). Human Development Reports. “Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and related indicators – India.” Accessed [date].  

---

## 8. UN – World Income Inequality Database (WIID, UNU-WIDER)

**What it’s good for:** A collection of inequality measures (Gini, income shares) from multiple sources, harmonized where possible.

### Web and downloads

- WIID portal:  
  https://www.wider.unu.edu/project/wiid-world-income-inequality-database

You can:

- Download the global dataset as:
  - Excel
  - Stata
  - CSV (depending on release)

No standard public REST API; integration is via bulk download.

**Citation example:**

> UNU-WIDER. World Income Inequality Database (WIID). Version [x.x]. “India country observations.” Accessed [date].  

---

## 9. OECD – Income Distribution Database (IDD) (limited for India)

**What it’s good for:** In-depth inequality measures for OECD and some partner countries. Coverage for India is limited or absent in many series, but worth checking if you need cross-country comparability.

### Web and downloads

- OECD Income Distribution Database:  
  https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=IDD

You can:

- Use the web interface to filter
- Download as:
  - CSV
  - Excel

### API

OECD has a powerful API:

Docs:  
https://data.oecd.org/api/sdmx-json-documentation/

Pattern:

```text
https://stats.oecd.org/SDMX-JSON/data/IDD/{LOCATION}.{INDICATOR}.{TIME}/all?contentType=csv
```

You would need to check whether India (`IND`) appears in the specific indicator you want.

---

## How to integrate these into your article

### 1. Decide on your “core” sources

For an article on poverty and inequality in India that needs clear, citable, and easily integrable statistics, a robust combination is:

- **World Bank WDI** – for headline poverty and Gini
- **World Bank PovcalNet** – for detailed poverty trends and international poverty lines
- **WID** – for top income/wealth shares and long-run inequality
- **MOSPI / NSS / PLFS** – for nationally produced, official statistics and microdata-based analysis
- **UNDP HDR** – for multidimensional poverty and inequality-adjusted measures

### 2. Example citation-ready “data blocks”

Here’s how you might structure a typical paragraph in your report (you’ll fill in the actual numbers from the sources above):

> According to the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, India’s Gini index of income inequality was X.X in YEAR (World Bank, WDI, indicator SI.POV.GINI). Using the international extreme poverty line of $2.15 a day (2017 PPP), the share of India’s population living in extreme poverty fell from Y.Y% in YEAR to Z.Z% in YEAR (World Bank, PovcalNet; WDI, indicator SI.POV.DDAY). Complementing these income-based measures, the latest Human Development Report estimates that A.A% of India’s population is multidimensionally poor, with an average intensity of deprivation of B.B% (UNDP, Human Development Reports, Multidimensional Poverty Index).

You can then add:

- A state-level breakdown using NITI Aayog SDG or MOSPI data.
- A narrative on top income shares using WID.

---

## Suggested follow-ups

- “Can you help me pick and extract a small set of specific indicators (with World Bank API URLs) for a time-series plot of poverty and inequality in India from 1990 to the latest year?”  
- “Could you walk me through how to use India’s NSS or PLFS microdata to compute my own poverty and Gini estimates, step by step in R or Python?”  
- “Can you help me reconcile differences between World Bank, WID, and MOSPI inequality figures for India and explain which is best for which type of argument?”

> According to the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, India’s Gini index of income inequality was X.X in YEAR (World Bank, WDI, indicator SI.POV.GINI). Using the international extreme poverty line of $2.15 a day (2017 PPP), the share of India’s population living in extreme poverty fell from Y.Y% in YEAR to Z.Z% in YEAR (World Bank, PovcalNet; WDI, indicator SI.POV.DDAY). Complementing these income-based measures, the latest Human Development Report estimates that A.A% of India’s population is multidimensionally poor, with an average intensity of deprivation of B.B% (UNDP, Human Development Reports, Multidimensional Poverty Index).

You can then add:

- A state-level breakdown using NITI Aayog SDG or MOSPI data.
- A narrative on top income shares using WID.
